opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because surgery is still, for many solid tumors, the best shot a patient has at a cure. But that doesn't mean it's the right answer for every patient. It's a huge intervention, and for some people the risks outweigh the benefits, or the cancer comes back so quickly that the surgery didn't buy them much.

So for me, rethinking surgery's place isn't about replacing it. It's about getting much better at deciding who should have it, when, and in combination with what. A lot of my work has been on liver cancer and liver metastases, where those decisions are hard. Surgeons are weighing how much liver can safely be removed, whether the patient will recover well, and whether the disease is likely to recur. Historically a lot of that has rested on clinical judgment and fairly coarse staging systems.

What excites me is that we're already collecting a lot of information we're not fully using. Every patient gets CT or MRI scans before surgery, and those images contain far more than a radiologist can describe. With quantitative imaging, what people call radiomics, and with machine learning, we can start pulling out patterns in tumor texture and in the surrounding tissue that may tell us about the tumor's biology. Then the question becomes whether those patterns can help predict who's likely to recur early, who might benefit from chemotherapy first, or who might do better with a less invasive approach.

The goal is to move from "this tumor is resectable, so we operate" to "given everything we know about this patient and this tumor, what's the treatment path most likely to help them?" Surgery stays central, but it becomes part of a more personalized plan instead of the default.

Of course, none of that matters unless it gets into clinical practice. That means models that are validated across institutions, that clinicians can trust and interpret, and that fit into how surgical teams actually make decisions. That's where I think the real work is now: bringing data science and the surgical community together so these tools change patient care, not just appear in papers.

r001.rationale: It says surgery remains the best chance of cure for many solid tumors and describes the traditional approach as operating when a tumor is resectable.

r002.rationale: It frames reconsidering surgery around deciding who should have it and when, including whether chemotherapy first or a less invasive approach would be better.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that surgery is still, for most solid tumors, the single most effective thing we can do for a patient. If you can take the tumor out completely, that's where cures actually come from. And yet surgery is in some ways the least studied part of cancer care. Drugs get randomized trials, biomarkers, companion diagnostics. Surgery gets a surgeon's judgment and a lot of experience, which is enormously valuable, but it isn't systematized in the way the rest of oncology has been.

So when I talk about rethinking surgery's place, I mean a few things. First, the decision of who should get an operation at all. Right now that decision is made largely on anatomy and whether the patient can tolerate it physiologically. But we have all this other information sitting there, imaging, pathology, genomics, the patient's history, and we're mostly not using it to ask the question that matters: is this person actually going to benefit? Some patients go through a major resection and recur within months. If we could have predicted that, we might have treated them differently, maybe started with systemic therapy, maybe spared them the operation altogether.

Second, the operation itself. There's a lot of variability in what happens in the room, and we don't measure it well. Margins, lymph node yield, how much normal tissue is removed. These things affect outcomes, and I think there's a real opportunity to bring data and modeling into the planning and execution so that the surgeon is working with more than what they can see and feel.

And third, honestly, it's about where surgery sits in the sequence. For a long time the model was operate first, then everything else. Now we're seeing that for some cancers, giving therapy before surgery changes the picture entirely. So surgery becomes one tool among several, timed deliberately, rather than the default starting point.

My background is in computer science, and I came to this working alongside surgeons at Memorial Sloan Kettering, and what struck me was how much their intuition was right but how little of it was captured anywhere. The goal isn't to replace that intuition. It's to give it a quantitative backbone so the decisions are more consistent, more personalized, and, frankly, more honest with patients about what an operation is likely to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response says complete tumor removal is where cures come from and describes “operate first, then everything else” as the longstanding model.

r002.rationale: It explicitly discusses treatment sequence, including whether therapy should come before surgery and surgery’s timing relative to other treatments.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move from asking, “Can we operate?” to asking, “Will this operation help this particular patient?” Surgery can be an incredibly powerful part of cancer treatment, but it’s also a major intervention. We need to understand how it fits with the biology of the disease, the other treatments available, and what matters to the patient.

That means looking beyond whether we can remove a tumor. Can we help someone live longer, and live well? Could they benefit from another treatment first? My interest is in how we can use data to make those decisions more precisely, so that we’re choosing the right treatment, for the right person, at the right time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether tumor removal helps a particular patient, but does not identify it as the prevailing paradigm for curing cancer.

r002.rationale: It asks whether a patient could benefit from another treatment first, framing surgery’s role partly as a question of treatment order.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to stop thinking of surgery as an isolated event and start thinking about where it fits in the whole course of a person’s cancer care. The question isn’t simply, “Can we remove this tumor?” It’s, “Will an operation help this patient, and when is the right time to do it?”

That means bringing together what we know from imaging, the tumor’s biology, and the patient’s response to treatment. AI could help us make better use of that information, but the goal is very human: choosing the treatment that gives someone the best chance of living longer and living well. Sometimes that will mean surgery, sometimes treatment before surgery, and sometimes avoiding an operation that won’t help.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether surgery will help and when to do it, but does not identify tumor removal as the prevailing paradigm for curing cancer.

r002.rationale: It frames surgery’s role around timing and treatment sequence, explicitly noting that treatment may come before surgery and that surgery may sometimes be avoided.
